bib.title: Language (Technology) is Power: A Critical Survey of “Bias” in NLP
bib.venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2020), pages 5454-5476

question: What do papers analyzing 'bias' in NLP systems mean by bias, why do they say it is harmful, and do their quantitative techniques match those motivations?
contributions: A survey of 146 papers on 'bias' in NLP, categorised by motivation and technique using an allocational/representational harms taxonomy
Finding that motivations are vague, inconsistent and lack normative reasoning, and techniques are poorly matched to motivations
Three recommendations (R1-R3) with concrete research questions
A case study on African-American English

results.claim: The survey covers 146 papers analyzing social bias in written-text NLP systems.
results.setup: ACL Anthology keyword search for bias/fairness before May 2020, plus citation-graph traversal; speech papers excluded

results.claim: Only 4 of 146 papers propose techniques for allocational harms, although 21% name them in their motivations.
results.setup: Manual categorisation of motivations and techniques with the allocational/representational harm taxonomy
results.quote: only four papers actually propose techniques
results.note: Table 2 gives 30 papers with allocational-harm motivations (30/146 is about 21%).

results.claim: 16% of papers give only vague motivations or none.
results.setup: Motivation categorisation; Table 2 lists 23 papers in Vague/unstated

results.claim: 32% of papers have no apparent normative concern, focusing on system performance instead.
results.quote: (32%) are not motivated by any apparent normative

results.claim: 16% of papers name immediate representational harms alongside more distant allocational harms.
results.setup: Motivation categorisation; downstream effects usually unmeasured

results.claim: Embeddings are the most studied task (54 papers), ahead of coreference resolution (20) and language modeling/dialogue generation (17).
results.setup: Table 1, counts do not sum to 146 since papers can cover several tasks
results.table: Table 1, row Embeddings (type-level or contextualized), column Papers

results.claim: By motivation, stereotyping has 50 papers, other representational harms 52, questionable correlations 47; by technique, stereotyping 58, other representational 43, questionable correlations 42, allocational 4, vague 0.
results.table: Table 2, row Stereotyping, columns Motivation 50 and Technique 58

limits: Survey of papers up to May 2020 only; written text only, speech excluded.
Categories overlap so counts do not sum to 146; categorisation was done by the authors' reading, with no inter-annotator agreement reported.
GAP shared-task papers were excluded from the vague/unstated and technique counts; Dabas et al. (2020) was excluded.
Predates LLM-era work: studies embeddings, coreference, MT, sentiment, toxicity, early LMs; says nothing on pretraining data curation or hallucination.
Does not measure any system; recommendations are qualitative and the research questions are explicitly non-comprehensive.
practices: R1: Ground bias work in literature outside NLP on language and social hierarchies, and treat representational harms as harmful in their own right (Sec 4, p5458).
R2: State explicitly why the system behaviors called bias are harmful, in what ways and to whom, and be open about the normative reasoning (Sec 4.2, p5460).
R3: Examine language use in practice by engaging the lived experiences of affected communities, and interrogate power relations between technologists and communities (Sec 4.3, p5460).
Reorient bias work around the question of how social hierarchies, language ideologies and NLP systems are coproduced (Sec 4.1, p5459).
Ask which linguistic norms, task definitions, data collection and annotation choices, and evaluation metrics shape a system, not only its predictions (Sec 4.1, p5459).
Ask whether a system should be built at all, rather than assuming it should exist (Sec 4.3, p5461).
